questions.title: Two signed roots
questions.prompt_html: Solve \(x^2+3x-28=0\). Give both roots.
questions.hint_html: Put the quadratic equal to zero before applying the zero-product rule.
questions.solution_html:
1. Find two numbers with product \(-28\) and sum \(3\): \(7\) and \(-4\).
  2. \((x+7)(x-4)=0\), so \(x=-7\) or \(x=4\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Find two numbers with product \(-28\) and sum \(3\): \(7\) and \(-4\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: The sign of a factor is not the sign of its root.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Solve \(x+7=0\) and \(x-4=0\) separately.

questions.title: Non-unit leading coefficient
questions.hint_html: Use a pair with product \(6(-5)=-30\) and sum \(-13\).
questions.solution_html:
1. Write \(-13x=-15x+2x\).
  2. \(6x^2-15x+2x-5=(3x+1)(2x-5)\).
  3. The zero-product rule gives \(x=-\frac13,\frac52\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: The coefficients of x still matter when solving each linear factor.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Divide by the coefficient of \(x\) in each factor.

questions.title: Do not cancel a solution
questions.prompt_html: Solve \(5x^2=15x\). Explain why dividing both sides by \(x\) can lose a solution.
questions.hint_html: Take out a common factor rather than dividing by the variable.
questions.solution_html:
1. Rearrange to \(5x(x-3)=0\).
  2. Therefore \(x=0\) or \(x=3\). Dividing by \(x\) would exclude the valid root \(0\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Therefore \(x=0\) or \(x=3\). Dividing by \(x\) would exclude the valid root \(0\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: Division by \(x\) silently assumed \(x\ne0\).
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Check \(x=0\) in the original equation.

questions.title: A rational equation
questions.prompt_html: Solve \(\frac{2x-1}{x+2}=x-1\), stating the excluded value first.
questions.hint_html: Record the denominator restriction before multiplying.
questions.solution_html:
1. The original expression requires \(x\ne-2\).
  2. \(2x-1=(x-1)(x+2)\), so \(x^2-x-1=0\).
  3. \(x=\frac{1\pm\sqrt5}{2}\); neither value is \(-2\), so both are valid.

marking_criteria.description_html: \(x=\frac{1\pm\sqrt5}{2}\); neither value is \(-2\), so both are valid.

misconceptions.feedback_html: A rearranged equation must still obey the original denominator restriction.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Write \(x\ne-2\), then check both candidates.

questions.title: A cancelled denominator
questions.prompt_html: Solve \(\frac{x^2-x-12}{x-4}=0\). Explain any rejected candidate.
questions.hint_html: A cancellation simplifies an expression but does not enlarge its domain.
questions.solution_html:
1. \(x\ne4\) and \(x^2-x-12=(x-4)(x+3)\).
  2. On the original domain the equation is \(x+3=0\). Hence \(x=-3\); the candidate \(4\) makes the original denominator zero.

marking_criteria.description_html: On the original domain the equation is \(x+3=0\). Hence \(x=-3\); the candidate \(4\) makes the original denominator zero.

misconceptions.feedback_html: At \(x=4\) the original fraction is undefined.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Cross out any candidate that makes the original denominator zero.

questions.title: Quadratic in a square
questions.prompt_html: Solve \(x^4-10x^2+9=0\) over the real numbers.
questions.hint_html: Treat \(x^2\) as a single variable, then return to \(x\).
questions.solution_html:
1. Let \(u=x^2\). Then \(u^2-10u+9=(u-1)(u-9)=0\).
  2. Thus \(x^2=1\) or \(x^2=9\).
  3. Taking both square-root signs gives \(x=\pm1,\pm3\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: Both positive and negative x-values can have the same square.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Use \(x=\pm\sqrt u\) for each positive \(u\).

questions.title: Reject a negative square
questions.prompt_html: Solve \(x^4+3x^2-4=0\) over the reals.
questions.hint_html: State the restriction on your substitution.
questions.solution_html:
1. Let \(u=x^2\ge0\): \((u+4)(u-1)=0\).
  2. Reject \(u=-4\), since a real square cannot be negative.
  3. \(x^2=1\), so \(x=\pm1\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Reject \(u=-4\), since a real square cannot be negative.

misconceptions.feedback_html: The second equation is \(x^2=-4\), not \(x^2=4\).
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Reject negative values of \(u=x^2\).

questions.title: Quadratic in a square root
questions.hint_html: After finding \(\sqrt{x}\), you still need to find \(x\).
questions.solution_html:
1. Let \(u=\sqrt{x}\ge0\). Then \(2u^2-5u+2=(2u-1)(u-2)=0\).
  2. \(u=\frac12\) or \(u=2\), both nonnegative.
  3. Since \(x=u^2\), the solutions are \(x=\frac14,4\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: These are values of \(\sqrt{x}\), not \(x\).
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Square each allowed value of \(u\).

questions.title: A negative substituted root
questions.prompt_html: Solve \(x+\sqrt{x}-6=0\). Explain why there is only one real solution.
questions.hint_html: Check the sign of \(u\) before squaring it.
questions.solution_html:
1. Let \(u=\sqrt{x}\ge0\). Then \((u+3)(u-2)=0\).
  2. Reject \(u=-3\), because the principal square root is nonnegative.
  3. \(u=2\) gives \(x=4\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Reject \(u=-3\), because the principal square root is nonnegative.

misconceptions.feedback_html: The candidate \(u=-3\) cannot equal \(\sqrt{x}\). Squaring it invents an extra answer.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Test \(x=9\) in the original equation.

questions.title: Two stages of substitution
questions.prompt_html: Solve \(\left(x+\frac1x\right)^2-5\left(x+\frac1x\right)+6=0\) over the reals. List distinct solutions only.
questions.hint_html: Solve the quadratic in \(u\), then solve a new quadratic in \(x\) for each \(u\).
questions.solution_html:
1. \(x\ne0\). Let \(u=x+\frac1x\); then \((u-2)(u-3)=0\).
  2. For \(u=2\), \(x^2-2x+1=0\), giving \(x=1\).
  3. For \(u=3\), \(x^2-3x+1=0\), giving \(x=\frac{3\pm\sqrt5}{2}\).
  4. All three values are nonzero. The repeated root \(1\) is listed once.

marking_criteria.description_html: All three values are nonzero. The repeated root \(1\) is listed once.

misconceptions.feedback_html: The values 2 and 3 solve the equation in the substituted expression, not in x.

questions.title: Find a repeated-root parameter
questions.prompt_html: Find \(k\) and the repeated root if \(x^2+10x+k=0\) has a repeated root.
questions.hint_html: Use \(\Delta=0\), then solve the resulting square.
questions.solution_html:

  2. The equation is \((x+5)^2=0\), with repeated root \(-5\).

questions.title: A parameter in the leading coefficient
questions.prompt_html: Find all real \(k\) for which \(kx^2+4x+1=0\) has two distinct real roots.
questions.hint_html: Check whether a parameter can remove the quadratic term.
questions.solution_html:
1. For a genuine quadratic, \(\Delta=16-4k\gt 0\), so \(k\lt 4\).
  2. Also require \(k\ne0\). At \(k=0\) the equation is linear and has only one root.

marking_criteria.description_html: Also require \(k\ne0\). At \(k=0\) the equation is linear and has only one root.

misconceptions.feedback_html: At \(k=0\) the equation is \(4x+1=0\), not a quadratic.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Remove \(k=0\) from the discriminant-based set.

questions.title: No real solutions
questions.prompt_html: Find all \(k\) such that \(2x^2-6x+k=0\) has no real roots.
questions.hint_html: A negative discriminant is required, not a non-positive one.
questions.solution_html:
1. No real roots requires \(\Delta=36-8k\lt 0\).
  2. Hence \(k\gt 36/8=9/2\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: At \(k=9/2\) there is a repeated real root.

questions.title: Two parameter values
questions.prompt_html: Find all \(k\) for which \(x^2-2kx+k+2=0\) has a repeated root, and give the repeated root in each case.
questions.hint_html: The discriminant is itself a quadratic in the parameter.
questions.solution_html:
1. \(\Delta=4(k^2-k-2)=4(k-2)(k+1)\).
  2. \(\Delta=0\) gives \(k=-1\) or \(k=2\).
  3. The repeated root is \(-b/(2a)=k\), giving the stated pairs.

marking_criteria.description_html: The repeated root is \(-b/(2a)=k\), giving the stated pairs.

misconceptions.feedback_html: Both factors of the discriminant can be zero.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Solve \((k-2)(k+1)=0\) completely.

questions.title: Exactly one is not always repeated
questions.prompt_html: Find all \(k\) for which \((k-1)x^2+2x+1=0\) has exactly one distinct real solution. Give that solution for each value of \(k\).
questions.hint_html: Check the linear case separately before setting the discriminant to zero.
questions.solution_html:
1. If \(k=1\), the equation becomes \(2x+1=0\), with root \(-1/2\).
  2. For \(k\ne1\), exactly one distinct root requires \(\Delta=4-4(k-1)=0\), so \(k=2\).
  3. At \(k=2\), \((x+1)^2=0\), so \(x=-1\).

marking_criteria.description_html: For \(k\ne1\), exactly one distinct root requires \(\Delta=4-4(k-1)=0\), so \(k=2\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: A linear equation can also have exactly one real solution.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Check \(k=1\) in the original equation.

questions.title: Tangency without calculus
questions.prompt_html: The line \(y=2x+c\) is tangent to \(y=x^2-6x+8\). Find \(c\) and the point of contact.
questions.hint_html: Use the discriminant of the intersection equation, not of the original curve.
questions.solution_html:
1. At an intersection, \(x^2-8x+8-c=0\).
  2. Tangency requires \(64-4(8-c)=0\), so \(c=-8\).
  3. The repeated root is \(x=4\); then \(y=2(4)-8=0\).

misconceptions.likely_wrong_answer_html: Using the discriminant of the curve alone.
misconceptions.feedback_html: Tangency concerns the solutions common to the line and curve.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Equate the two expressions for \(y\) first.

questions.title: Always above the axis
questions.prompt_html: Find all \(k\) for which \(x^2+2kx+k+3\gt 0\) for every real \(x\).
questions.hint_html: The inequality in the parameter is another quadratic inequality.
questions.solution_html:
1. The leading coefficient is positive. Strict positivity for all x requires \(\Delta=4(k^2-k-3)\lt 0\).
  2. The boundary values are \(k=(1\pm\sqrt{13})/2\).
  3. The quadratic in k is negative between the roots, with endpoints excluded.

marking_criteria.description_html: The leading coefficient is positive. Strict positivity for all x requires \(\Delta=4(k^2-k-3)\lt 0\).
The quadratic in k is negative between the roots, with endpoints excluded.

misconceptions.feedback_html: The quadratic in k opens upwards, so it is negative between its roots.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Test \(k=0\), which makes the original expression \(x^2+3\gt 0\).

questions.title: Remove an interior exceptional value
questions.prompt_html: Find all \(k\) for which \((k-2)x^2-4x+k-2=0\) has two distinct real roots.
questions.hint_html: The discriminant interval may contain a value that is not quadratic.
questions.solution_html:
1. \(\Delta=16-4(k-2)^2\gt 0\) gives \((k-2)^2\lt 4\).
  2. Hence \(0\lt k\lt 4\).
  3. Exclude \(k=2\), since the equation then becomes \(-4x=0\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: At \(k=2\), only the linear equation remains.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Split the interval at the forbidden value.

questions.title: The leading coefficient also matters
questions.prompt_html: Find all real \(k\) for which \((k-1)x^2+2kx+k+3\gt 0\) for every real \(x\).
questions.hint_html: For an expression to be strictly positive everywhere, check its orientation as well as its roots.
questions.solution_html:
1. If \(k\lt 1\), the graph opens downwards and cannot stay positive. If \(k=1\), it is \(2x+4\), which also cannot stay positive.
  2. Thus require \(k\gt 1\) and \(\Delta=4[\,k^2-(k-1)(k+3)\,]=4(3-2k)\lt 0\).
  3. The discriminant condition gives \(k\gt 3/2\), which already implies \(k\gt 1\).

marking_criteria.description_html: If \(k\lt 1\), the graph opens downwards and cannot stay positive. If \(k=1\), it is \(2x+4\), which also cannot stay positive.
The discriminant condition gives \(k\gt 3/2\), which already implies \(k\gt 1\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: A downward-opening quadratic with no roots is negative everywhere, not positive.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Check the sign of \(k-1\) and the linear case.

questions.prompt_html: Solve \(x^2-4x-1\le0\), giving exact endpoints.
questions.hint_html: A squared-distance inequality bounds x on both sides.

1. \(x^2-4x-1=(x-2)^2-5\).
  2. \((x-2)^2\le5\) gives \(-\sqrt5\le x-2\le\sqrt5\).
  3. Add 2 to all three terms. Both endpoints are included.

questions.hint_html: A squared distance at least a positive number gives two exterior regions.

  2. Hence \(x-1\le-3\sqrt2/2\) or \(x-1\ge3\sqrt2/2\).
  3. Add 1 and retain the two exterior intervals, including equality.

misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Test the midpoint to choose the correct side.

questions.title: Intersect two quadratic conditions
questions.prompt_html: Solve simultaneously \(x^2-x-12\le0\) and \(x^2-4\gt 0\).
questions.hint_html: Draw the two solution sets on the same number line.
questions.solution_html:
1. The first inequality gives \((x-4)(x+3)\le0\), hence \(-3\le x\le4\).
  2. The second gives \(x\lt -2\) or \(x\gt 2\).
  3. The intersection is \([-3,-2)\cup(2,4]\).

misconceptions.feedback_html: Simultaneously means both conditions must hold.
misconceptions.repair_hint_html: Shade only the overlap; keep each endpoint’s own strictness.

questions.title: One interval must contain another
questions.prompt_html: Find all real \(k\) such that \((x-k)^2\le4\) is true for every \(x\) in \([-1,3]\).
questions.hint_html: Compare the left endpoints and the right endpoints.
